title: Esthetic Judgment
summary: How to judge a work by what it does as art, which is not the same as agreeing with its philosophy.

lessons.title: Two different questions
lessons.objective: Separate an esthetic judgment of a work from a philosophical agreement with its ideas.

exercises.prompt: What does an esthetic judgment ask about a work?

choices.text: What it does as art
Whether you vote with its author
Whether the price is high
Whether the artist is famous

feedback.note: Esthetic judgment looks at the work as art. Agreement, price, and fame are different questions.

exercises.prompt: Agreeing with a work’s stated ideas is which kind of judgment?

choices.text: A philosophical judgment
Already a full esthetic judgment
A market forecast
A biography of the artist

feedback.note: Sharing a philosophy answers whether you accept the ideas. It does not by itself grade the work as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to the kind of judgment it is.

pairs.left: Does this painting hold together as a painting?
Is the novel’s theory of history true?
Did the sculpture make one whole in its medium?

feedback.note: Questions about the work as art stay esthetic. A question about whether a theory is true is philosophical.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit’s distinction.

parts.text: Judge the work by what it
as art, not by whether you

feedback.note: The two blanks name the split: performance as art on one side, agreement on the other.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the split.

feedback.note: The judgment and the agreement are neighbors that people mix. They are not the same act.

exercises.prompt: A reader who rejects a novel’s ideas can still do what?

choices.text: Judge whether the novel succeeds as art
Skip judgment, because disagreement ends the question
Treat disagreement as proof the art failed
Copy the ideas in order to be fair

feedback.note: Rejection of the philosophy leaves the esthetic question open. It does not answer it.

exercises.prompt: Which remark mixes the two questions?

choices.text: I disagree, so the book is bad as art.
I disagree, and I still have to judge the art.
The ideas are one issue. The work as art is another.
I can answer each question on its own.

feedback.note: Disagreement is not an esthetic grade. Using it as one collapses the two questions.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it can play.

pairs.left: Liking the message
A clear whole in the medium
A true premise in a separate essay

feedback.note: Only what the work does as art supplies the esthetic evidence. Approval and a side essay do not.

exercises.prompt: Complete the pair of verdicts one person can hold.

parts.text: You can praise the work as

feedback.note: The two verdicts are allowed to differ. Praise of the art is not a signature under the philosophy.

exercises.prompt: Which line is the rule of this unit?

choices.text: Judge the work by what it does as art.
Judge the work by the club the artist joins.
Judge the work by your mood that afternoon.
Judge the work by how old it is.

feedback.note: Club, mood, and age are not the standard. The standard is what the work does as art.

lessons.title: What the work does as art
lessons.objective: Judge by the selective re-creation the work actually presents, not by a slogan placed beside it.

exercises.prompt: As art, what is the work supposed to have done?

choices.text: Presented a selective re-creation, formed as one work
Listed every fact about its subject
Won a vote for a party
Hidden its subject so nothing can be seen

feedback.note: The esthetic question looks for a selective re-creation that stands as a work, not a dump of facts or a campaign.

exercises.prompt: A slogan in the preface, while the work itself is muddled, counts as what?

choices.text: Not a substitute for what the work does
A repair of the work as art
The whole esthetic judgment
The medium of the work

feedback.note: A line beside the work can announce an intention. It cannot do the work’s job for it.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to where it belongs in the judgment.

pairs.left: What is selected and how it is formed
An interview about intentions
The critic’s party membership

feedback.note: Judgment stays on the re-creation in the work. Talk around it, and the critic’s politics, are not that re-creation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the warning about labels.

feedback.note: A label can name a hope. The esthetic fact is what the work itself does.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction for this lesson.

feedback.note: The object of judgment is the re-creation on the page, the stage, or the wall, not a caption or a rumor.

exercises.prompt: A painting is judged esthetically by which of these?

choices.text: What the image presents and how it is made
The wall text alone
Who gave the museum the painting
How soft the gallery bench is

feedback.note: The image is the work. A wall text can help a visitor, but it is not the painting.

exercises.prompt: Two works share a message. What follows for esthetic judgment?

choices.text: They can still differ in what they do as art
They must be equal as art
Neither can be judged
The longer one wins

feedback.note: A shared message does not settle the art. Each work is graded by the re-creation it presents.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to what it does as art.

pairs.left: A selective whole that embodies its view
A pile of true facts with no selection
A caption that states the moral for a blank canvas

feedback.note: Truth in a pile, or a moral in a caption, is not yet a selective re-creation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the comparison of two works that share a creed.

feedback.note: The creed can be the same while the works are not. Follow the work.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, “what it does as art” means which of these?

choices.text: What it accomplishes as a selective re-creation
How many ads it sells
How many years the artist spent
How much ink the printer used

feedback.note: Time, ink, and sales are not the accomplishment. The accomplishment is the re-creation the work achieves.

lessons.title: Skill is not a vote
lessons.objective: See that artistic skill and agreement with a philosophy can come apart in either direction.

exercises.prompt: A work is highly skilled, and you reject its philosophy. What can you say?

choices.text: It can be strong as art while you reject the view
Skill forces you to accept the view
Rejection forces the skill to count as zero
Skill is not allowed in a work you reject

feedback.note: Skill is about what the work does as art. It does not cast your vote on the philosophy.

exercises.prompt: You accept the philosophy, and the work is clumsy as art. What follows?

choices.text: Agreement does not make the work good art
Agreement repairs the clumsiness
Clumsiness proves the philosophy is false
You must hide the clumsiness

feedback.note: A welcome philosophy cannot stand in for a re-creation the work failed to achieve.

exercises.prompt: Match each split to the fair description.

pairs.left: Skilled projection of a view you reject
pairs.right: Strong as art, disputed as philosophy

pairs.left: Clumsy projection of a view you accept
pairs.right: Welcome as philosophy, weak as art

pairs.left: Treating skill as a vote for the ideas
pairs.right: A mix-up of the two questions

feedback.note: Each direction of the split is possible. Only the third line confuses skill with agreement.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about what skill is evidence of.

feedback.note: A ballot chooses a view. Skill shows what the work accomplished as art.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that keeps skill off the ballot.

feedback.note: You can record the skill and withhold agreement. The skill did not vote.

exercises.prompt: Which report is a fair split?

choices.text: The play is well made, and I still reject its view of man.
The play is well made, so I must accept its view of man.
I reject the view, so the making does not count.
Well made and true-for-me are the same phrase.

feedback.note: The fair report keeps the making and the view in separate columns.

exercises.prompt: Which report is unfair to the art?

choices.text: I share the moral, so the drawing must be good.
I share the moral, and I still look at the drawing.
I share the moral, and the drawing is still weak.
Sharing the moral leaves the drawing to be judged.

feedback.note: A shared moral is not a grade for the drawing. The drawing still has to do its job.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two verbs you may use together.

parts.text: the ideas in the same work.

feedback.note: Admire names the esthetic side. Reject names the philosophical side. Both can stand.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to what it is.

pairs.left: Admiring the craft
Rejecting the ideas
Treating admiration as agreement

feedback.note: Admiration is not a signature. Calling it agreement mixes the two responses.

lessons.title: Theme through the means
lessons.objective: Ask whether the theme is carried by the work’s own means, rather than by a lecture standing in for the art.

exercises.prompt: When does a theme belong inside an esthetic judgment?

choices.text: When the work’s own means carry it
When a footnote states it and the work does not
When a friend explains it after you leave
When a trend says themes are fashionable

feedback.note: The theme counts as part of what the work does only if the means of that work carry it.

exercises.prompt: A lecture stands in for the story, and the story never embodies the point. What is that, as art?

choices.text: A failure to do the job, even if the lecture is true
A success, because truth repairs any story
The best use of a story’s means
Something esthetic judgment must ignore

feedback.note: A true speech is still a speech. If it replaces the art, the work has not done its job as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the judgment it supports.

pairs.left: The theme is shown in the action
pairs.right: The means are doing the work

pairs.left: The theme is announced, and the action never supports it
The medium is ignored so a message can be delivered
pairs.right: The work is not being judged as art

feedback.note: Support inside the work is the test. An announcement, or a message that skips the medium, is not that test.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule about theme and means.

feedback.note: Through the means is the esthetic path. Around them is a lecture wearing the work’s name.

exercises.prompt: Build the warning about a true sentence.

feedback.note: Truth of a sentence is a philosophical point. It does not become the art by being true.

exercises.prompt: How is a novel’s philosophy relevant to the esthetic question?

choices.text: Only as what the novel must make real in its own story
Only if it is a view you already hold
Only if a character states it at the greatest length
It can never appear in the story at all

feedback.note: The philosophy matters esthetically as the theme the story concretizes, not as a view you prepaid for.

exercises.prompt: In this lesson, what is the failure called when art is used only as a slot for a speech?

choices.text: Letting a lecture replace the means
Selecting and forming a re-creation
Keeping esthetic and philosophical questions apart
Showing skill you do not agree with

feedback.note: The failure is substitution: the speech does the talking, and the means of the art do not.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to its role.

pairs.left: An image that embodies the meaning
A note that tells you what to feel while the image is mud
Your prior agreement with the meaning
pairs.right: Not a means of the work

feedback.note: Embodiment is the painting’s job. A scolding note, and your prior agreement, are not means of that painting.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test.

parts.text: the theme, the work has not

feedback.note: Carry and done name the test: the means either achieve the theme as art, or they do not.

exercises.prompt: Which question closes this lesson?

choices.text: Do this work’s means actually carry its theme?
Does the author belong to my club?
Is the speech the longest chapter?
Is the theme true, and can I stop there?

feedback.note: Stop on the means. Club membership, length, and bare truth do not answer whether the work carried its theme.

lessons.title: One standard, applied
lessons.objective: Apply the same esthetic standard to works you welcome and works you oppose.

exercises.prompt: You dislike the philosophy. What happens to the esthetic standard?

choices.text: It stays the same
It is dropped
It reverses so failure counts as success
It becomes your mood

feedback.note: Dislike changes your philosophical answer. It does not rewrite the esthetic standard.

exercises.prompt: You love the philosophy. What happens to the esthetic standard?

choices.text: It stays the same
It softens so any effort counts as success
It no longer applies
It becomes loyalty to the author

feedback.note: Love of the ideas is not a softer ruler. The work is still judged by what it does as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the right move.

pairs.left: A work you love that is poorly made
pairs.right: Say so under the esthetic standard

pairs.left: A work you oppose that is strongly made
pairs.right: Say so under the same standard

pairs.left: A work you have not taken in

feedback.note: The standard applies in both directions, and only to a work you have actually taken in.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule of application.

parts.text: for works you welcome and works you

feedback.note: Welcome and oppose are philosophical postures. They share one esthetic standard.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction to keep the ruler steady.

feedback.note: Either way means when you agree and when you do not. Softer and louder are not the standard.

exercises.prompt: Which report keeps the questions apart?

choices.text: As art it fails to integrate, though I agree with the author.
As art it fails because I disagree.
As art it succeeds because I agree.
I never say what it does as art.

feedback.note: The first report gives the art its own grade and the philosophy a separate one.

exercises.prompt: Which report collapses the two questions?

choices.text: It fails as art because I disagree.
It is strongly made, and I disagree.
It is weakly made, and I agree.
I ask what it does as art before I grade it.

feedback.note: Because I disagree is a philosophical reason dressed up as an esthetic grade.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to its job.

pairs.left: What does it do as art?
Do I agree?
Which question am I answering?

feedback.note: Name the question first. Then the grade lands on art or on agreement, not on a blur of both.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing instruction.

feedback.note: Apart means each judgment gets its own answer: what the work does as art, and whether you agree.
